questions.q: Why does a computer need primary storage?
options: The CPU can only work on data and instructions that are in main memory
Primary storage keeps files safe when the power is off
Primary storage is cheaper per gigabyte than secondary storage
Primary storage holds the operating system permanently
questions.feedback: The CPU reaches main memory directly. Anything on a drive has to be loaded into it first.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.2 Lesson 1 — Memory bay, station 1: Why primary storage?

questions.q: State what is meant by primary storage.

markPoints.concept: memory the CPU can access directly
markPoints.exemplar: Memory the CPU can access directly.

questions.example: Memory that the CPU can access directly, such as RAM and ROM.
questions.paraphrase: The memory the processor reads from straight away.
questions.feedback: Directly accessible by the CPU is the definition; RAM and ROM are the examples.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.2 Lesson 1 — Memory bay, station 1: Why primary storage?

questions.q: A hard disk is an example of primary storage.
options: True
False
questions.feedback: False. A hard disk is secondary storage. Primary storage is RAM and ROM.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.2 Lesson 1 — Memory bay, station 1: Why primary storage?

questions.q: Which statement about RAM is true?
options: It is volatile, so its contents are lost when the power is switched off
It is non-volatile, so its contents survive a restart
It can only be read from, never written to
It holds the instructions that start the computer up
questions.feedback: RAM is volatile and is read from and written to constantly. The start-up instructions are in ROM.

questions.paraphrase: It stands for random access memory.
questions.feedback: Random access memory. 'Read-and-write memory' describes it but is not what the letters stand for.

questions.q: Explain what is meant by saying that RAM is volatile.

markPoints.concept: its contents are lost when the power is removed
markPoints.exemplar: Everything in RAM is lost when the power is switched off.

markPoints.concept: so anything that must be kept has to be saved to secondary storage
markPoints.exemplar: So anything that has to be kept must be saved to secondary storage.

questions.example: RAM is volatile, which means everything in it is lost as soon as the power is switched off, so anything that needs to be kept has to be saved to secondary storage first.
questions.paraphrase: Its contents disappear when the computer is turned off, so work has to be written to a drive if you want it afterwards.
questions.feedback: Volatile means lost without power. The second mark is for what follows from it.

options: The instructions the computer needs to start up
The programs the user is running now
The user's documents and photographs
Data that has been swapped out of RAM
questions.feedback: ROM holds the boot program, which runs before anything can be loaded from a drive.

questions.q: Give one reason the start-up instructions are kept in ROM rather than RAM.

markPoints.concept: ROM is non-volatile, so they are still there when the power comes on
markPoints.exemplar: ROM is non-volatile, so the instructions are still there when the computer is switched on.

questions.example: ROM is non-volatile, so the instructions are still there when the power comes back on. RAM would be empty.
questions.paraphrase: ROM keeps its contents without power, and RAM does not.
questions.feedback: If the boot instructions were in RAM there would be nothing to run when the computer was switched on.

questions.q: ROM is normally much smaller than RAM.
options: True
False
questions.feedback: True. ROM only has to hold the start-up instructions, so it is measured in megabytes while RAM is measured in gigabytes.

questions.q: Sort each statement by whether it describes RAM or ROM.
items: Holds the programs currently in use
Written to constantly while the computer runs
questions.feedback: Volatile and busy is RAM; non-volatile and small is ROM.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.2 Lesson 1 — Memory bay, station 4: RAM vs ROM

markPoints.concept: RAM is volatile; ROM is non-volatile
markPoints.exemplar: RAM is volatile and ROM is non-volatile.

markPoints.concept: RAM holds what is in use now; ROM holds the start-up instructions
markPoints.exemplar: RAM holds the programs in use while ROM holds the start-up instructions.

markPoints.concept: RAM is read from and written to; ROM is normally only read
accept: written to|read/write|readwrite|can be changed|can be overwritten|writable|both read
read only|only read|cannot be written|not written|cannot be changed
markPoints.exemplar: RAM can be written to, while ROM is normally only read.

markPoints.concept: RAM is much larger than ROM
markPoints.exemplar: RAM is much larger than ROM.

questions.example: RAM is volatile while ROM is non-volatile, so RAM empties when the power goes and ROM does not. RAM holds the programs and data in use at the moment, while ROM holds the instructions that start the computer. RAM is written to constantly, while ROM is normally only read. RAM is also far larger, measured in gigabytes against a few megabytes of ROM.
questions.paraphrase: RAM empties when the power goes and ROM does not. RAM stores whatever software is running and is changed all the time, while ROM stores the boot instructions and is only read. There is also far more RAM than ROM.
questions.feedback: A comparison needs both sides of each point. Four differences, each naming what RAM does and what ROM does.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.2 Lesson 1 — Memory bay, station 4: RAM vs ROM

questions.q: Put the steps of starting a computer in order.
steps: The operating system is loaded from secondary storage into RAM
The user's programs can be loaded into RAM
questions.feedback: ROM first, because it is the only memory with anything in it when the power comes on.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.2 Lesson 1 — Memory bay, station 5: The boot sequence

questions.q: Explain why the operating system has to be copied into RAM when a computer starts.

markPoints.concept: the CPU can only work on data and instructions that are in RAM
markPoints.exemplar: The CPU can only work on instructions that are in RAM.

markPoints.concept: and the operating system is stored on secondary storage, which the CPU cannot run from
markPoints.exemplar: It is kept on the hard disk, so it has to be copied across before it can run.

questions.example: The CPU can only execute instructions that are in RAM, and the operating system is stored on secondary storage, so it has to be copied into RAM before any of it can run.
questions.paraphrase: The processor only runs what is in main memory, which means the operating system has to be loaded there from the drive first.
questions.feedback: The CPU's reach is the reason. The drive is where the operating system lives the rest of the time.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.2 Lesson 1 — Memory bay, station 5: The boot sequence

questions.q: A computer with 4 GB of RAM is slow when several large programs are open. Why would adding more RAM help?
options: More programs can be held in RAM at once, so less has to be swapped to secondary storage
The CPU will complete more cycles each second
The hard disk will spin faster
The operating system will need fewer instructions
questions.feedback: More RAM does not make the CPU faster. It reduces how often the computer has to use the much slower drive.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.2 Lesson 1 — Memory bay, station 6: More RAM, faster computer?

questions.q: A computer already has far more RAM than it ever uses. Explain why adding more would make almost no difference.

markPoints.concept: everything that is needed already fits in RAM
accept: already|enough|fits|never full|not full|spare|unused|plenty|nothing is being|room to spare
markPoints.exemplar: Everything that is needed already fits in RAM.

markPoints.concept: so nothing is being swapped out, and there is nothing for the extra RAM to prevent
accept: virtual memory|swapped out|swap space|swapping|paging|secondary storage|pushed out|trips to the disk|slow trips
markPoints.exemplar: So virtual memory is never being used, and the extra RAM has nothing to prevent.

questions.example: If everything the computer needs already fits in RAM, it is never having to swap anything out to virtual memory, so extra RAM has nothing to prevent and the computer is no faster.
questions.paraphrase: Because nothing is being pushed out to the disk in the first place, more memory has no slow trips to save and makes no difference.
questions.feedback: More of something you are not short of changes nothing. The mark is for saying what the extra RAM would have been preventing.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.2 Lesson 1 — Memory bay, station 6: More RAM, faster computer?
